draft.title: Short-term borrowing
card: Short-term borrowing is money borrowed for a short time, usually less than a year, to pay for day-to-day needs such as wages, stock and bills.
Overdraft
lets a business draw out more than it has in its bank account, up to an agreed limit. Interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn.
Commercial bill
a short-term loan where the business issues a bill promising to pay a set sum on a set date. It is sold at a discount and repaid at its full face value.
Factoring

selling the business's accounts receivable (money customers owe it) to a factor for immediate cash, less a fee. The factor then collects the debts. These sources are quick to arrange but can cost more.
draft.remember: Short-term borrowing covers daily needs quickly, but often costs more.

a.q: Which source of finance gives a business immediate cash by selling the money its customers owe it?
a.why: Factoring means selling accounts receivable to a factor for cash now, less a fee. An overdraft is tempting, but it lets the business draw more than its balance up to a limit and does not involve selling customer debts.
a.clue: Think about whose debts are being sold.

b.q: Priya's florist in Ballarat has a quiet week and is short of cash to pay wages on Friday. Her bank account will be a little overdrawn for a few days. Which source best suits this need?
opts: An overdraft with an agreed limit
A commercial bill sold at a discount
A bank loan paid back over many years
b.why: An overdraft is quick to arrange and interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn, so it suits a brief shortfall in the account. Factoring is tempting, but it works by selling money customers owe, and a florist serving mostly walk-in customers has few such debts to sell.
b.clue: Which source covers a small, brief gap in the bank balance?

b.best: An overdraft with an agreed limit
